metadata.title: Returns to Skills Around the World (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the OECD PIAAC adult skills survey (collected 2011–2012) and applies post-sampling weightings in the estimations throughout, as stated in the PIAAC data description. The analytic sample is restricted to prime-age (35–54) full-time wage and salary workers (at least 30 hours/week), excluding self-employed workers, and trimming the bottom and top 1% of the wage distribution within each country to limit outliers. Because the paper reports using sample weights in the estimations, the results are intended to be representative of the adult population within each participating country under the survey design. No replicate-weight method (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported in the provided text, so uncertainty estimation details cannot be extracted here.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that it uses the first plausible value of the PIAAC domain scores in regression analyses, but it does not describe how missing questionnaire or earnings/skill data were handled (e.g., complete-case deletion vs imputation). This is a reporting gap because PIAAC typically contains item nonresponse and missing background variables, and the choice of missing-data strategy can affect estimated skill–earnings gradients and cross-country comparisons. The provided text therefore does not allow a defensible mapping to a specific missing-data handling method.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PIAAC adult skills data for 22 countries (excluding Australia and the Russian Federation; excluding problem-solving domain participation in Cyprus, France, Italy, and Spain). The baseline analytic sample is restricted to prime-age workers aged 35–54, who are full-time employees (at least 30 hours/week), excluding self-employed workers. Wage and earnings are measured as gross hourly earnings of wage and salary workers; for countries with only decile-reported earnings in the public use file, decile medians are assigned to participants. Within each country, the bottom and top 1% of the wage distribution are trimmed to reduce outlier influence. The paper also notes that this full-time/prime-age restriction may understate total skill effects if skills also affect employment probabilities.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses the PIAAC 2011–2012 adult skills survey to estimate how cognitive skills relate to labor-market earnings across the full working life, focusing in the baseline on prime-age (35–54) full-time wage and salary workers in 22 countries. Skills are measured in literacy, numeracy, and problem solving on 500-point scales, standardized within countries, and the regressions use the first plausible value of each domain score. A one-standard-deviation increase in numeracy is associated with about a 17.8% (≈18%) higher hourly wage on average across countries, with substantial heterogeneity: returns exceed 21% in six countries (largest in the United States at ~28%) and are below 15% in eight countries (including all Nordic countries). The paper reports robustness to alternative earnings measures (continuous vs decile medians; inclusion of bonuses; hourly vs monthly; adding self-employed) and to additional controls (e.g., parental education, migrant status, occupation/industry). Cross-country institutional patterns show systematically lower skill returns in countries with higher union density, stricter employment protection, and larger public-sector shares, while product-market regulation and minimum wages show weaker or conditional relationships. The study emphasizes that these associations are best interpreted as lower bounds due to measurement error in skills and that causal interpretation is not established.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD working paper using econometric regression models (Mincer-style wage equations with skill measures and controls) rather than a machine-learning predictive modeling pipeline. The provided text does not report any ML algorithms, model-selection metrics, or ML-based prediction targets, so ml_techniques and main_findings are intentionally left empty per the schema rules for non-ML empirical papers.
